name.text: Amplitude phase angle and mean line from a graph

questiontext.text:
The graph shows the wave \(y = a\sin(x + c) + d\), where \(a \gt 0\) and \(-180^\circ \lt c \lt 180^\circ\).

[[jsxgraph width="520px" height="300px"]] (function() { // static board: grid, axes and one wave; x in degrees var xl = -180, xr = 360, yl = {#ylo#}, yu = {#yhi#}; var b = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, {boundingbox: [xl - (xr-xl)*0.04, yu, xr + (xr-xl)*0.02, yl], axis: false, grid: false, showNavigation: false, showCopyright: false, pan: {enabled: false}, zoom: {enabled: false}}); var g = {strokeColor: '#dddddd', strokeWidth: 1, fixed: true, highlight: false}; for (var gx = Math.ceil(xl/(15))*(15); gx <= xr + 1e-9; gx += 15) { b.create('segment', [[gx, yl], [gx, yu]], g); } for (var gy = Math.ceil(yl/(0.5))*(0.5); gy <= yu + 1e-9; gy += 0.5) { b.create('segment', [[xl, gy], [xr, gy]], g); } var ax = {strokeColor: '#000000', strokeWidth: 1, fixed: true, highlight: false}; b.create('segment', [[xl, 0], [xr, 0]], ax); b.create('segment', [[0, yl], [0, yu]], ax); var t = {fixed: true, highlight: false, useMathJax: false, fontSize: 11, anchorX: 'middle', anchorY: 'top'}; for (var tx = Math.ceil(xl/(60))*(60); tx <= xr + 1e-9; tx += 60) { if (Math.abs(tx) > 1e-9) { b.create('text', [tx, -(yu-yl)*0.015, String(Math.round(tx*10)/10) + '\u00b0'], t); } } var ty = {fixed: true, highlight: false, useMathJax: false, fontSize: 11, anchorX: 'right', anchorY: 'middle'}; for (var tv = Math.ceil(yl/(1))*(1); tv <= yu + 1e-9; tv += 1) { if (Math.abs(tv) > 1e-9) { b.create('text', [-(xr-xl)*0.01, tv, String(Math.round(tv*10)/10)], ty); } } b.create('functiongraph', [function(x) { return ({#a#})*Math.sin(Math.PI*(x+({#cc#}))/180)+({#d#}); }, xl, xr], {strokeColor: '#1f4e9c', strokeWidth: 2, fixed: true, highlight: false}); })(); [[/jsxgraph]]
(a) Find the amplitude \(a\). [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]
(b) Find the phase angle \(c\). [[input:ans2]] \(^\circ\) [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]
(c) Find \(d\), where \(y = d\) is the mean line. [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]] [[feedback:prt3]]

generalfeedback.text:
The greatest value is \({@amax@}\) and the least is \({@dmin@}\).

(a) The amplitude is half of (greatest \(-\) least): \(a = {@a@}\).

(c) The mean line is halfway between: \(d = {@d@}\).

(b) The wave crosses its mean line going up at \(x = {@nc@}^\circ\). \(y = \sin x\) does this at \(0^\circ\), so the wave is \(y = \sin x\) moved {@dir@} by \({@abs(cc)@}^\circ\): the phase angle is \(c = {@cc@}^\circ\).

The wave is \(y = {@a@}\sin(x {@tc(cc)@}^\circ){@tc(d)@}\).

questiondescription.text:
Trigonometry III: amplitude, phase angle and mean line from a graph

Grade 12 CBE Core 2.5: Read the amplitude, phase angle and mean line of y = a sin(x + c) + d from its graph in degrees.

Core

This question is original to this project.

truefeedback.text: That is the greatest value of \(y\). The amplitude is half of (greatest \(-\) least).
That is greatest minus least. Halve it.

falsefeedback.text: Read the greatest and least values of \(y\) from the graph. The amplitude is half of (greatest \(-\) least).

truefeedback.text: Your angle gives the same wave, but give the phase angle between \(-180^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\).

Test your value: \(y = a\sin(x + c) + d\) crosses its mean line going up where \(x + c = 0^\circ\). With \(c = {@ans2@}^\circ\) that is at \(x = {@-ans2@}^\circ\). Where does the graph cross its mean line going up?
That is where a maximum is. Use the point where the wave crosses its mean line going up, and compare it with \(0^\circ\) for \(y = \sin x\).

falsefeedback.text: Test your value: \(y = a\sin(x + c) + d\) crosses its mean line going up where \(x + c = 0^\circ\). With \(c = {@ans2@}^\circ\) that is at \(x = {@-ans2@}^\circ\). Where does the graph cross its mean line going up?

truefeedback.text: You added the greatest and least values. The mean line is halfway: halve the sum.

falsefeedback.text: The mean line is halfway between the greatest and least values of \(y\). Test yours: the greatest value minus \({@ans3@}\) is \({@nice(amax-ans3)@}\), and \({@ans3@}\) minus the least value is \({@nice(ans3-dmin)@}\). On the mean line these two are equal.

qtest.description: Greatest value; sign of c; sum not halved
Greatest minus least; c outside the range; greatest value
